messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Miguel's Story

Miguel Reyes was twenty-two when the pneumatic nail gun slipped from his grip on a Tuesday morning in March. He had been working on a new residential complex in the North Hills, installing metal studs alongside his supervisor, Dennis, a man he'd worked with for nearly two years. The day had been routine—Miguel had arrived at six in the morning, grabbed coffee from the site trailer, and was already three hours into the job when it happened. He was securing a header frame, the nail gun held at chest height, when his palm began to sweat. He'd been thinking about his mother's birthday party that weekend, distracted for just a moment, and the tool rotated in his hand. The nail fired at an angle. It caught Dennis in the upper thigh, missing the femoral artery by what the emergency room doctor later said was perhaps two centimeters.

The sound of Dennis screaming had a particular quality—not pain exactly, but shock and disbelief. Miguel had stood frozen, watching the blood bloom across his supervisor's work pants, and in that moment something in his mind had fractured. He had not been careless in the way that careless people are careless. He had been present, had been trained, had been careful every other day of his life. But on this day, in this second, his body had betrayed him. His hands had done something his mind had never intended. For months afterward, Miguel would replay that instant obsessively, turning it over and over in his mind like a stone worn smooth by constant handling. What if he had gripped the gun differently? What if he had not thought about his mother? What if he had positioned himself at a different angle? The questions spiraled without resolution, each cycle leaving him more exhausted than the last.

Dennis survived. The doctors repaired the wound, and he returned to work eight weeks later. But Miguel could not return to the site. The very thought of standing in that space, of holding a pneumatic tool, sent his heart racing and made his palms slick with sweat. His supervisor had offered him a desk role, administrative work, but Miguel found that even entering the office building made his chest tight. The fluorescent lights, the smell of the break room coffee—things that had once been neutral—now triggered a visceral sense of dread. He had come to believe that his body was fundamentally unreliable, that it could betray him without warning, that he could not trust his own hands to do what he commanded them to do.

What frightened him most was silence. When the job site fell quiet, when there were no sounds of saws or drills, Miguel felt certain that something catastrophic was about to happen. In the absence of noise, danger seemed imminent. He began to avoid any situation that might be stressful—he declined invitations from friends, stopped going to his gym, avoided even the minor friction of traffic by staying home. His apartment became his refuge, the one place where he felt he had any control. He had stopped going to the grocery store because the fluorescent aisles and the unpredictable crowds felt unsafe. His sister brought him food now. She had stopped asking him when he was coming back to work.

The memory itself felt strange to him, as if it belonged to someone else entirely. When he tried to recall the moment, he could smell the metallic tang of the blood, could feel the texture of the grip tape on the nail gun, but the person in that memory—the one who had let the tool slip—did not feel like himself. He had become someone unrecognizable, someone capable of hurting another person through his own failure. He could not forgive himself for not doing more to stop it, even though logically he understood that the accident had taken less than a second.

Last week, Miguel's mother had asked him to see someone. The anniversary of the incident was approaching in three weeks, and she had noticed him becoming more withdrawn, more rigid with anxiety. He had agreed, not because he believed talking would change anything, but because he could no longer bear the weight of what he had done, or the person he had become in the aftermath.
